---
title: Query and traverse the graph
description: Ask the graph what it actually knows — match triple patterns with dockg query, walk edges with dockg traverse, and find out what depends on a page before you move it.
---

import { Aside, CardGrid, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`dockg stats` answers aggregate questions. This page is for the specific ones — *what points at
this page? what does changing it reach? did that concept land the way I wrote it?*

Both commands are read-only and exit `0` even when nothing matches. They are for exploring, not
gating.

## Before you start

A built graph. Every example below runs against
[`test/fixtures/corpus/`](https://github.com/hawkeyexl/dockg/tree/main/test/fixtures/corpus), so
your IRIs will differ — the shapes will not.

## Which command answers which question

| Question | Command |
|---|---|
| Show me every X | `dockg query` — match a triple pattern, omit a term for a wildcard |
| What is connected to this node | `dockg traverse` — walk edges from a starting point |

Readers reach for the wrong one first. `query` is a filter over the whole graph; `traverse` is a
walk from somewhere.

## `dockg query`

Give it a subject, predicate, object, or any combination. Whatever you omit is a wildcard.

```sh
dockg query -p dcterms:title
```

```
<https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md> dcterms:title "Configuration Reference"
<https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md#advanced> dcterms:title "Advanced"
<https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md> dcterms:title "Getting Started"
<https://example.com/kg/product/sp-x100> dcterms:title "SP-X100"

16 match(es)
```

Everything the graph asserts about one node:

```sh
dockg query -s "https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md"
```

```
<…/configuration.md> iirds:has-topic-type <http://iirds.tekom.de/iirds#GenericReference>
<…/configuration.md> iirds:relates-to-product-variant <https://example.com/kg/product/sp-x100>
<…/configuration.md> dcterms:references <https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md>
<…/configuration.md> dcterms:subject <https://example.com/kg/concept/configuration>
<…/configuration.md> dcterms:title "Configuration Reference"
```

Filter by type:

```sh
dockg query -p rdf:type -o dockg:Section
```

<Aside type="tip" title="CURIEs, not full IRIs">
  `dcterms:title` rather than `http://purl.org/dc/terms/title`. The prefix table is fixed and
  emitted with every graph, so the short form is always safe. See the
  [vocabulary reference](/dockg/reference/vocabulary/) for which predicate to ask for.
</Aside>

Objects that are literals match verbatim:

```sh
dockg query -p dcterms:title -o "Getting Started"
```

## `dockg traverse`

Walk from a node. Default depth is one hop.

```sh
dockg traverse "https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md"
```

```
https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md — Getting Started
  iirds:GenericTask
  iirdsSft:Deployment
  https://example.com/kg/agent/person/jane-doe
  https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md#getting-started — Getting Started
  https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md — Configuration Reference
  https://example.com/kg/concept/installation

10 nodes, 10 hops, 0 excluded
```

### What points at this page?

Follow inbound edges, narrowed to link edges:

```sh
dockg traverse "https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md" \
  --reverse --predicates dcterms:references
```

```
https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md — Getting Started
  https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md — Configuration Reference

2 nodes, 1 hop, 0 excluded
```

**Run this before you move, rename, or delete a page.** It is the whole reason link derivation
exists, and it is the question `stats` cannot answer for one specific file.

### What does changing this reach?

```sh
dockg traverse "https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/getting-started.md" --impact
```

```
  https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md — Configuration Reference
  https://example.com/kg/activity/build
    https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/windows-notes.md — Windows Notes
    https://example.com/kg/graph

4 nodes, 7 hops, 0 excluded
```

<Aside type="caution" title="`--impact` changes the depth default">
  From 1 to 3. If you are comparing an `--impact` run against a plain one, that difference is the
  flag doing two things, not one.
</Aside>

## Scope filters, and reading what they excluded

```sh
dockg traverse "https://example.com/kg/product/sp-x300" \
  --reverse --depth 2 --variant SP-X300
```

```
https://example.com/kg/product/sp-x300 — SP-X300

excluded by scope:
  https://example.com/kg/doc/docs/configuration.md — dockg:notApplicableToVariant https://example.com/kg/product/sp-x300

1 node, 1 hop, 1 excluded
```

**Read the exclusions line, not just the nodes.** A filter that returns plausible results while
excluding nothing is indistinguishable from no filter at all — and that is the failure
[open-world semantics](/dockg/concepts/open-world/) warns about, one layer up.

A variant that is not in the graph is an error rather than an empty result:

```
dockg: Unknown product variant: SP-X999 — no iirds:ProductVariant matches that IRI, title, or slug.
```

Exit `2`. An unresolvable filter would otherwise return exactly what it was meant to exclude.

<Aside type="note" title="`rdf:type` is not followed by default">
  Every document shares `dockg:Document`, so walking type edges would make every document reachable
  from every other in two hops. If a traversal looks narrower than you expected, this is usually
  why — and it is deliberate.
</Aside>

## Verifying what you modelled

<Steps>

1. **Check a concept converged the way you intended.** Slug convergence is silent by design: two
   spellings become one node.

   ```sh
   dockg query -p skos:prefLabel
   ```

2. **Check a hierarchy is the shape you wrote.**

   ```sh
   dockg query -p skos:broader
   ```

3. **Check applicability landed**, including the negative side.

   ```sh
   dockg query -p dockg:notApplicableToVariant
   ```

</Steps>

## Scripting it

Both commands take `--format json` for stable, machine-readable output:

```sh
dockg query -p dcterms:references --format json > references.json
```

For anything more involved than a pattern match, use the
[library API](/dockg/reference/library-api/) — `runQuery` and `runTraverse` return structured
results, and `GraphIndex` gives you the index directly.

## What you have now

A way to answer questions about one specific node rather than the corpus as a whole — and the
impact check to run before changing a page anything else depends on.
